name: oe-kimi-F-S-P
finalResponse:
The brief says "repositioning," which usually means an agency's mood film, a sans-serif logo, a hashtag nobody asked for, and an apology by the third quarter. What follows is a slower suggestion: this is not a brand that needs to become something else — it is a brand that needs to be caught being itself, in rooms where the young can watch. Loosely held, as always. The quote-tweets grade the homework.

Notice first that high awareness with falling under-35 share is not obscurity; it is a verdict. They know exactly who you are and have filed you under *other people*. You don't argue with a verdict; you introduce new evidence. And notice that the two past failures — mocked by the young, alienated the base — were not two failures. They were one event seen from opposite ends of the aisle: the brand was caught pretending. The young mock performance; the base mourns betrayal; both are reacting to the same insincerity. Which means the fix is not a balancing act. It is a subtraction.

**The agency's deck is a photograph of someone else's youth.** The last campaigns counted impressions and assumed the rest — permission, relevance, the conversion they claimed. So build your own baseline first: purchase by cohort, organic mention volume and tone, search terms, resale and thrift presence, and the pockets where the brand is *already* bought young — there is always a pocket. Relevance cannot be proven against a baseline that was never kept. Run the counterfactual honestly, too: doing nothing is not free, it just sends the invoice slowly, at the rate of the actuarial table. Then make the agency's model the agency's problem — brief for earned outcomes, pay against lift in organic mention and cohort repeat, not against reach. Reach is the one thing this brand already owns.

**Change the context, not the codes.** The positioning, in one line: *the original, unchanged on purpose — the one your grandmother was right about.* In a category that rebrands every eighteen months, standing still is the loudest move available; permanence reads as counterculture to a generation raised on drops and pivots. Preserve the product's truth — and audit it first, because if quality was quietly cheapened across the decades, restore it before any storytelling; the story is only allowed to be true. Preserve the mark, the packaging codes, the color that means *us* on the shelf, the founder's actual words, the factory, the jingle — as archive, not anthem. Retire the youth slang, the borrowed celebrities, the meme-chasing, the apologetic tone, and any sentence containing "not your father's" — a construction that insults the father and bores the child. Retire the word "modernization" internally; it has a body count. The test for every element: would a customer of thirty years nod, and would a stranger of twenty-five not laugh? Both, or it doesn't ship.

**The archive is the R&D department.** Heritage is not a costume; it is receipts. Seventy years of packaging, ads, founder letters, factory footage — release it as found material, deadpan, no grand campaign around it. Limited archive editions in the original packaging, the original language: scarcity with provenance. Let design-literate young people mine it and feel the pleasure of the find, because that pleasure is the whole mechanism. A generation does not want to be handed relevance; it wants to make a discovery. You cannot hand someone their own discovery. You can only leave the door open and the lights on.

**Be discovered, not delivered.** The channel plan follows from that. Where the base lives — the shelf, the circular, the familiar broadcast — nothing changes; the codes stay, the voice stays. Where the young live, the brand appears only in third person: product seeded with people who have their own credibility and no script, stocked on the counters where taste is made rather than the feeds where reach is sold, present in the small rooms the baseline says are already buying. The brand's own voice goes archival and dry — answers questions when asked, never announces its own coolness. And the single best content asset is already on payroll: the person who has made or inspected the product for thirty years. Hand them a camera, not a script. The base will love it because it is true; the young will love it because it is plainly not for them — which is the same reason. *Who on the floor has been there longest, and why has no one filmed them?*

**Win the first match where nobody is watching.** Sequence by evidence, not ambition. The data will show a green shoot — a city, a campus, a counter, a community that adopted the brand years ago without permission. Water that; plant nothing new. Six months of quiet seeding and archive drops in that one place, measured against the baseline: organic mentions, cohort repeat, the tone of the quote-tweets. Only when third parties are telling the story unprompted does paid media return — saying what is already true, pointing at what people already found. Advertising that announces a discovery nobody made is how the last two campaigns died. And study those campaigns like a competitor's fire: you already bought the consulting; it is sitting in the screenshots.

**The loyal base is the evidence, not the obstacle.** Young consumers do not trust brands that hide their old customers; they trust brands whose old customers visibly refuse to leave. So the covenant goes public early: nothing you love is leaving — the classic stays, the formula stays, any change announced before it ships. Then put the base on camera: the thirty-year customers, the family three generations deep. To the base it reads as respect; to the young it reads as provenance. Same footage, two truths. When packaging must evolve, run old and new in parallel until the new one begs to be left alone — no big-bang cutover. The base forgives faster than the young forget; treat both facts as assets.

**Give the argument a test instead of a vote.** The internal fight — how much change can the brand absorb — dissolves once you separate the layers: identity, which absorbs none; expression, which absorbs renovation; channel, which absorbs a rebuild. Each faction has been fighting over a different layer and calling it one fight. Hand a small team the archive keys and the baseline, supervise loosely, and let evidence settle what meetings won't. And put a named human on the tripwires — base retention, mockery ratio, repeat rate of the young cohort — with authority to pause anything that tests well but smells wrong. Testing well but smelling wrong is precisely how the last campaigns got made. *Whose job is it to flinch?*

**Count what the mood film can't see.** The dashboard will want awareness among 18–34; the brand has awareness — it has a verdict. Count instead: organic mention volume and tone, earned-to-owned ratio, cohort repeat purchase, searches for the brand next to the words "vintage" and "archive," presence in resale, the age mix of new buyers at full price — and base retention, which is the payback wearing a suit. Grade quarterly against the counterfactual, with the numbers owned by someone whose bonus doesn't depend on them. The soft signals arrive first: the creator who tags the brand without being paid, the quote-tweets turning fond, the grandchild who buys it as a gift and means it. If the green shoot cannot show the shape of relevance in two seasons, the national push does not get bought. That is not caution; it is the whole design.

One thing worth sitting with: the brief lists relevance and loyalty as if they were in tension — the future on one side of the ledger, the past on the other. Enter through the authenticity door and they become one line item. The young were never asking the brand to be young; they were asking it to be real, and they can smell the difference at sixty frames per second. The base was never asking it to stay old; they were asking it to stay itself. Same request, different
